title: Entropy shaper: burst window and graceful fallback PRD notes
summary: Working notes for a tenant-adaptive "entropy shaper" that bounds bursty tenant behaviour with a time-windowed credit decay, plus a companion graceful-fallback fabric that enables predictable isolation without hard evictions. Goal: reduce noisy-neighbor incidents and unpredictable latency spikes while preserving burstability for real product-driven peaks.
problem_statement: Dedicated pools today struggle with short, high-QPS spikes from a small number of tenants that cause transient tail latency and emergency preemptions. Existing approaches either: 1) strictly cap tenants (hurts genuine product bursts), or 2) overprovision to absorb spikes (costly). We need a middle ground that: honors short bursts for legitimate workloads, limits chronic noisy tenants, and provides deterministic, observable fallback behavior for clients.
goals: Allow short-term bursts that map to real product events (signup rushes, live events) without manual intervention
Automatically damp chronic noisy tenants over minutes-to-hours while preserving user-visible SLAs
Provide deterministic fallback routing for overflow traffic (lower-cost model variants, queued soft-lane, or graceful throttling) with clear metrics
Expose actionable telemetry (burst credits, entropy score, fallback triggers) in Console and API for ops and customers
non_goals: Replace long-term billing/commitment models (reserved capacity economics remain separate)
Full-blown RL-based autoscaler in this phase (we'll keep heuristic + statistical models)
Guaranteeing zero tail latency for every tenant under extreme multi-tenant storms
assumptions: Most harmful noisy patterns are identifiable by short-term entropy in request rate + variance in sequence length
We can approximate per-tenant memory/kv-cache pressure via request-key cardinality heuristics
Routing layer already supports policy-based fallbacks to model variants and regions
Customers can tolerate a defined soft-degradation path during sustained overloads (they prefer predictable degraded output over opaque failures)
user_stories: As an SRE, I want automatic burst credit decay so recurring noisy tenants are progressively de-prioritized without manual eviction
As a platform engineer, I want an observable entropy score per tenant in Console so I can debug noisy-neighbor incidents
As a customer, I want short signup-driven bursts to succeed without being rate-limited, but sustained abusive traffic to be routed to the cheaper model variant
As a product manager, I want a clear SLA contract that defines when fallbacks are triggered so we can communicate with customers
autoscaling_algorithm: We keep the cluster-level autoscaler (existing predictive warm-pool + on-demand grow) but augment per-tenant shaping with a two-layer control: 1) Burst window ledger: each tenant accrues "burst credits" based on recent baseline rate. Credits replenish slowly (configurable half-life), and each request consumes credits proportional to compute weight (tokens * model-cost). 2) Entropy shaper: a short-window volatility metric (e.g., coefficient of variation over 30s) increases a temporary penalty multiplier that raises effective credit consumption for highly volatile tenants. Rationale: reward steady predictable load, allow one-off bursts, and throttle noisy variance. Implementation notes: ledger stored in Redis shard with soft expiry, TTL tuned to window size; entropy calc computed in routing layer via rolling counters. Tunables: window size (default 5m), replenishment half-life (default 15m), volatility sensitivity (default 0.8).
burst_window_design: Key idea: map bursts to a sliding time window instead of absolute per-second caps. Each tenant has a window budget W (in compute-units). Budget is refilled on an exponential schedule: W(t+dt)=W(t)+alpha*(max_baseline - W(t)). On request, we compute cost C and deduct C * penalty. If budget > 0, allow immediate routing; if budget falls below a soft threshold, tag request for fallback lanes. Rationale: windows smooth microbursts while allowing ramp events. Additive features: burst tax — a small extra cost for consecutive bursts to disincentivize repeated microbursts (helps fairness).
isolation_controls: Isolation should be gradual and observable. Controls: 1) Soft lanes: once tenant budget below threshold, new requests are routed to a soft lane: (a) cheaper/quantized model variant, (b) prefetched cached prefixes, or (c) queue with short delay (default 200-800ms). 2) Priority decay: tenant priority is decayed proportional to sustained budget deficit. 3) Tenant heal window: after deficit period, priority recovers slowly to prevent oscillation. 4) Crowd-shielding policy: if a pool-level storm is detected, shield smallest/highest-entropy tenants first rather than random eviction.
fallback_and_degradation: Fallback fabric choices (ordered): 1) local model-variant fallback (lower-cost quantized runtime) 2) regional fallback (route to secondary dedicated pool in different region if capacity) 3) soft-queue with client-backoff hint 4) best-effort streaming with truncated output. Each fallback emits an explicit reason code surfaced to SDK and Console. We propose a 'degradation policy' object per tenant that operators can configure via Console: preferred fallback order, min_quality thresholds, and max-fallback-duration. SDKs should surface backoff hints so clients can adapt (e.g., exponential client retry with jitter).
metrics_and_slos: Tail-latency p99/p999 before and after fallback (histogram)
SLO: <5% of requests for committed tenants should hit fallback under normal traffic; under surge, fallback <= 20% for 15min windows
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (canary): implement ledger + entropy metrics, collect signals on 4 small dedicated pools (1 week)
Phase 1 (soft-enforce): enable tagging and Console visibility; no automatic fallback, but annotate requests and notify customers via webhooks (2 weeks)
Phase 2 (auto-fallback opt-in): enable fallback fabric for opted-in customers with conservative tunables + SLA guardrails (4 weeks)
Phase 3 (default enabled): after 6 weeks of stable telemetry and customer opt-ins, flip default and expose multi-tenant controls in Console
ops_runbook_notes: Quick runbook highlights: if pool noisy_neighbor_events spike, check top entropy_score tenants -> examine burst_credit_balance -> if fallback is too aggressive, increase replenishment alpha or widen window. Emergency rollback: flip routing policy to 'legacy-strict-caps' feature-flag. Alerting: >3x baseline noisy_neighbor_events for >2m -> paging to on-call.
security_and_compliance: No customer data stored in ledger beyond tenant id and counters. Ledger uses internal service account with KMS-encrypted Redis. Fallback to another region must follow existing cross-region compliance policies; provide opt-out in tenant settings for geo-restricted workloads.
open_questions: What exact compute-unit normalization should we use across model families? (token-cost vs. measured GPU-ms)
How to provide clear billing semantics when fallback routes to cheaper or more expensive variants? (should be transparent on invoice)
Should tenants be able to purchase 'burst credits' as add-on? (possible upsell)
Edge-case: long-tailed batched workloads that look like steady but cause cache eviction — do we need cache-pressure signals?
